title: Ναυσικάας ὄνειρος καὶ πλυνοί
titleEn: Nausicaa’s Dream and the Washing-Day — Odyssey 6.1–109
about: While Odysseus sleeps, Athena goes to the Phaeacians. The poem first tells how they came to live at Scheria under Nausithous, and that Alcinous now rules. Athena enters the bedchamber of his daughter Nausicaa in the likeness of a friend, scolds her for neglecting her clothes now that marriage is near, and bids her go to the river at dawn to wash. In the morning Nausicaa asks her father for a wagon and never mentions marriage; he understands and gives it. The girls load the wagon, wash the clothes at the river, spread them on the shore, bathe, eat, and play ball, and the part ends on the simile that sets Nausicaa among her attendants like Artemis among her nymphs.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὁ μὲν ἔνθα καθεῦδε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ὕπνῳ καὶ καμάτῳ ἀρημένος·
sentences.l:
So he indeed there was sleeping, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
by sleep and by weariness worn down;
sentences.i: So much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus lay sleeping there, worn down by sleep and by weariness;
sentences.n: The book opens on Odysseus asleep. ὁ is 'he': in Homer the article is a pronoun, and ὁ μέν here looks ahead to αὐτάρ in the next line ('he indeed slept, but Athena …'). καθεῦδε is an imperfect of καθεύδω 'sleep' without the augment. πολύτλας δῖος is Odysseus’ stock pair of epithets, 'much-enduring, heavenly'. ἀρημένος is a participle of uncertain formation whose sense, 'worn down, afflicted', is sure.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀθήνη
βῆ ῥ’ ἐς Φαιήκων ἀνδρῶν δῆμόν τε πόλιν τε,
sentences.l:
but Athena
set out then for the Phaeacian men’s land and city both,
sentences.i: But Athena went to the land and city of the Phaeacians,
sentences.n: βῆ ῥ’ is βῆ ῥα: βῆ is an unaugmented aorist (Attic ἔβη) and ῥα a weak particle 'then', elided before ἐς. Φαιήκων ἀνδρῶν is a genitive plural, 'of the Phaeacian men'. δῆμος is the land and people of a community and πόλις the town itself; τε … τε joins them.

sentences.t:
οἳ πρὶν μέν ποτ’ ἔναιον ἐν εὐρυχόρῳ Ὑπερείῃ,
ἀγχοῦ Κυκλώπων ἀνδρῶν ὑπερηνορεόντων,
οἵ σφεας σινέσκοντο, βίηφι δὲ φέρτεροι ἦσαν.
sentences.l:
who formerly once dwelt in Hypereia of wide dancing-grounds,
near the Cyclopes, men over-bold,
who used to harm them, and in might were stronger.
sentences.i: They had once lived in spacious Hypereia, near the overbearing Cyclopes, men who kept harming them and were stronger in might.
sentences.n: The clause explains why the Phaeacians live where they do. εὐρυχόρῳ, 'of wide dancing-grounds', is built on χορός 'dancing-place' and means roomy; the literal sense is kept in `l`. Κυκλώπων ἀνδρῶν: the Cyclopes are called 'men' here. ὑπερηνορεόντων is an uncontracted participle (Attic -οῦντων) of ὑπερηνορέω, from ὑπέρ 'over' and ἠνορέη 'manliness', so 'being over-manly, swaggering'. σινέσκοντο is the iterative form (with -σκ-) of σίνομαι 'harm', 'used to harm', and σφεας is 'them'. βίηφι has the ending -φι, which does the work of an instrumental: 'by might'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν ἀναστήσας ἄγε Ναυσίθοος θεοειδής,
εἷσεν δὲ Σχερίῃ, ἑκὰς ἀνδρῶν ἀλφηστάων,
ἀμφὶ δὲ τεῖχος ἔλασσε πόλει, καὶ ἐδείματο οἴκους,
καὶ νηοὺς ποίησε θεῶν, καὶ ἐδάσσατ’ ἀρούρας.
sentences.l:
From there, having made them rise, led them Nausithous, godlike-in-form,
and settled them in Scheria, far from gain-winning men,
and around the city he drove a wall, and he built houses,
and made temples of the gods, and divided plough-lands.
sentences.i: Nausithous, godlike in form, moved them from there and led them away, and settled them in Scheria, far from men who earn their living; he ran a wall round the city, built houses, made temples for the gods, and divided the plough-lands.
sentences.n: ἄγε is unaugmented (= ἦγε). θεοειδής is 'godlike in form' (θεός + εἶδος 'shape'). εἷσεν is the aorist of ἵζω in its causative sense, 'made sit, settled'; Σχερίῃ is a dative of place, 'in Scheria', with no preposition. ἀνδρῶν ἀλφηστάων: the genitive plural in -άων (= -ῶν) of ἀλφηστής, whose meaning is not certain. It is usually derived from ἀλφάνω 'find, earn, gain', hence 'men who earn their living'; some ancient readers took it as 'grain-eating'. ἀμφὶ … ἔλασσε is a tmesis (a preverb standing apart from its verb): 'drove a wall around'. ἐδείματο is from δέμω 'build', ἐδάσσατ’ from δατέομαι 'divide among themselves'; ἄρουρα is 'plough-land'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν ἤδη κηρὶ δαμεὶς Ἄϊδόσδε βεβήκει,
Ἀλκίνοος δὲ τότ’ ἦρχε, θεῶν ἄπο μήδεα εἰδώς.
sentences.l:
but he already, by his doom overcome, had gone to Hades’,
and Alcinous then ruled, from the gods counsels knowing.
sentences.i: But Nausithous had already been overcome by his doom and gone to the house of Hades, and Alcinous now ruled, a man who knew counsels from the gods.
sentences.n: ὁ μέν is 'he', Nausithous, set against Ἀλκίνοος δέ. The first line is word for word 3.410. Ἄϊδόσδε has the suffix -δε of direction: 'to Hades’ (house)', as in οἶκόνδε. κηρί is the dative of κήρ 'doom'; δαμείς is the aorist passive participle of δάμνημι 'overpower'; βεβήκει is a pluperfect, 'had gone'. θεῶν ἄπο: the preposition stands after its noun (its accent thrown back), 'from the gods'. μήδεα εἰδώς, 'knowing counsels', uses the perfect participle of οἶδα; here the counsels come from the gods.

sentences.t:
τοῦ μὲν ἔβη πρὸς δῶμα θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
νόστον Ὀδυσσῆι μεγαλήτορι μητιόωσα.
sentences.l:
To his, then, set out to the house the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena,
planning a homecoming for great-spirited Odysseus.
sentences.i: To Alcinous’ house went the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, contriving a homecoming for great-spirited Odysseus.
sentences.n: τοῦ is the article as a pronoun in the genitive, 'his' (Alcinous’), placed first before πρὸς δῶμα for emphasis. Ὀδυσσῆι is a dative; the poet has forms with -σσ- and -σ- (Ὀδυσσῆος beside Ὀδυσῆος) as the metre needs. μεγαλήτορι is the stock epithet 'great-spirited'. μητιόωσα, from μητιάω 'devise', is an uncontracted form (Attic μητιῶσα) built on μῆτις 'cunning intelligence'.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ἐς θάλαμον πολυδαίδαλον, ᾧ ἔνι κούρη
κοιμᾶτ’ ἀθανάτῃσι φυὴν καὶ εἶδος ὁμοίη,
Ναυσικάα, θυγάτηρ μεγαλήτορος Ἀλκινόοιο,
sentences.l:
She set out to go to the much-wrought chamber, in which a maiden
was sleeping, to the immortal ones in stature and form like,
Nausicaa, daughter of great-spirited Alcinous,
sentences.i: She set out for the richly wrought bedchamber where a maiden lay sleeping, like the goddesses in stature and form, Nausicaa, the daughter of great-spirited Alcinous,
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἴμεν, literally 'she went to go', is a stock way of saying 'she set out'; ἴμεν is the infinitive of εἶμι 'go' in its epic -μεν ending. ᾧ ἔνι stands for ἐν ᾧ: the preposition follows its relative pronoun, with its accent thrown back. κοιμᾶτ’ is κοιμᾶτο, imperfect of κοιμάομαι 'sleep'. ἀθανάτῃσι is a feminine dative plural in -ῃσι, 'the immortal women', that is the goddesses; φυήν and εἶδος are accusatives of respect, 'in stature and in form'. The name comes last, in the third line.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δὲ δύ’ ἀμφίπολοι, Χαρίτων ἄπο κάλλος ἔχουσαι,
σταθμοῖιν ἑκάτερθε·
sentences.l:
and beside her two attendants, from the Graces beauty having,
at the doorposts on either side;
sentences.i: and beside her were two attendants, who had their beauty from the Graces, one at each doorpost;
sentences.n: πάρ is παρά with its last vowel dropped; there is no verb, 'and beside her, two attendants'. Χαρίτων ἄπο: the preposition follows its noun, 'from the Graces' (the Χάριτες, goddesses of grace and beauty); with κάλλος ἔχουσαι it means 'having their beauty from the Graces'. σταθμοῖιν is a dual dative in -οιιν, 'at the two doorposts'; ἑκάτερθε has the place-suffix -θε, 'on either side'.

sentences.t: θύραι δ’ ἐπέκειντο φαειναί.
sentences.l: and the shining doors were set to.
sentences.i: The shining doors were shut.
sentences.n: ἐπέκειντο, from ἐπίκειμαι 'lie upon, be set against', is the usual way to say that a door is shut. φαειναί is the feminine plural of φαεινός 'shining', the word kept as 'shining' in this part.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἀνέμου ὡς πνοιὴ ἐπέσσυτο δέμνια κούρης,
στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς, καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν,
εἰδομένη κούρῃ ναυσικλειτοῖο Δύμαντος,
ἥ οἱ ὁμηλικίη μὲν ἔην, κεχάριστο δὲ θυμῷ.
sentences.l:
And she, like a blowing of wind, rushed to the bedding of the maiden,
and she stood then above her head, and to her spoke a word,
resembling the daughter of ship-famous Dymas,
who was of like age with her, and was dear to her in heart.
sentences.i: She rushed to the maiden’s bed like a breath of wind, stood over her head and spoke to her, taking the likeness of the daughter of Dymas, famous for his ships, a girl of her own age who was dear to her at heart.
sentences.n: ἡ is 'she', Athena. ἐπέσσυτο is an aorist middle of ἐπισεύομαι 'rush upon'; δέμνια is the neuter plural for the bedding, 'the bed'. Line 21, στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς, καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν, is word for word 4.802; ἔειπεν is a form of εἶπον with an epic doubled ε. εἰδομένη, from εἴδομαι 'make oneself like', takes the dative κούρῃ: 'resembling the girl'. ναυσικλειτοῖο 'famous for ships' has κλειτός, the same word as κλυτός 'famous'. ὁμηλικίη is an abstract noun used of a person, 'a contemporary, an age-mate'; οἱ is 'to her'. κεχάριστο, pluperfect of χαρίζομαι 'please, gratify', has the sense 'was dear', with θυμῷ 'in her heart'.

sentences.t: τῇ μιν ἐεισαμένη προσέφη γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: Having made herself like to her, addressed gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Gleaming-eyed Athena, making herself like her, spoke to her:
sentences.n: ἐεισαμένη is the aorist middle participle of εἴδομαι 'make oneself like', with an epic lengthened ἐ-; it takes the dative τῇ 'to her'. μιν, 'her', is Athena herself: 'having made herself like to that girl'. προσέφη is the house reply-verb 'addressed'. The colon introduces Athena’s speech, lines 25–40.

sentences.t: Ναυσικάα, τί νύ σ’ ὧδε μεθήμονα γείνατο μήτηρ;
sentences.l: “Nausicaa, why then you so slack did your mother bear?
sentences.i: “Nausicaa, why did your mother bear you so careless?
sentences.n: τί νύ is 'why then'; νύ is a particle of urgency. σ’ is σε 'you', elided. ὧδε is 'so, thus'. μεθήμονα, 'slack, remiss', is built on μεθίημι 'let go, slacken'. γείνατο, from γείνομαι 'bring forth, bear', is an unaugmented aorist; the Greek has no 'your', only μήτηρ. The question is a scolding: a girl of her station should not be careless, and what follows says why.

sentences.t:
εἵματα μέν τοι κεῖται ἀκηδέα σιγαλόεντα,
σοὶ δὲ γάμος σχεδόν ἐστιν, ἵνα χρὴ καλὰ μὲν αὐτὴν
ἕννυσθαι, τὰ δὲ τοῖσι παρασχεῖν, οἵ κέ σ’ ἄγωνται.
sentences.l:
Clothes indeed for you lie uncared-for, glossy,
and for you marriage near is, when it is needful fine things yourself
to put on, and others to those to provide, who may take you as bride.
sentences.i: Your glossy clothes lie neglected, and your marriage is near, when you must dress yourself in fine things and provide others for those who are to take you as bride.
sentences.n: εἵματα is a neuter plural with a singular verb, κεῖται, as is regular. ἀκηδέα is 'uncared for' (ἀ- + κῆδος 'care'). σιγαλόεντα, 'glossy', is used of fine cloth and rugs here and of reins in line 81; its exact sense is not quite certain. ἵνα here means 'when, in which case', not 'so that'. ἕννυσθαι and παρασχεῖν depend on χρή. τοῖσι is the article as a pronoun, 'to those'; κέ with the subjunctive ἄγωνται makes it indefinite, 'whoever may take you'; ἄγομαι, 'lead to oneself', is the verb for taking a wife.

sentences.t:
ἐκ γάρ τοι τούτων φάτις ἀνθρώπους ἀναβαίνει
ἐσθλή, χαίρουσιν δὲ πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ.
sentences.l:
For from these things a report to men goes up,
good, and they rejoice, father and lady mother.
sentences.i: For from these things a good report reaches men, and your father and lady mother are glad.
sentences.n: τοι is a particle here, 'you see', a form of the pronoun σοι. φάτις, from φημί, is 'talk, report', here the good talk about a bride who is well turned out. ἀνθρώπους ἀναβαίνει is 'goes up to men'. ἐσθλή, 'good', stands at the start of its line. πότνια μήτηρ is 'lady mother'.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴομεν πλυνέουσαι ἅμ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι·
sentences.l: But let us go, to wash, at the same time as appearing dawn;
sentences.i: But let us go and do the washing as dawn appears;
sentences.n: ἴομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive (Attic ἴωμεν), 'let us go'. πλυνέουσαι is the future participle of πλύνω, uncontracted (Attic πλυνοῦσαι), giving purpose: 'to wash'. ἠοῖ is the dative of ἠώς 'dawn', and φαινομένηφι has the ending -φι, which does the work of a dative or instrumental: 'with dawn appearing'. Athena speaks as a friend and puts the plan as a shared one.

sentences.t:
καί τοι ἐγὼ συνέριθος ἅμ’ ἕψομαι, ὄφρα τάχιστα
ἐντύνεαι, ἐπεὶ οὔ τοι ἔτι δὴν παρθένος ἔσσεαι·
sentences.l:
and I as fellow-worker along with you will go, so that most quickly
you may make ready, since not for long any more a maiden will you be;
sentences.i: and I will go along with you as a helper, so that you may get ready as quickly as possible, since you will not be a maiden much longer;
sentences.n: συνέριθος is 'fellow worker, helper'. ἕψομαι is the future of ἕπομαι 'follow'; ἅμα is an adverb here, 'along'. ὄφρα takes the subjunctive ἐντύνεαι, with Ionic -εαι for -ῃ: 'so that you may get yourself ready'. ἔσσεαι is the epic future of εἰμί (Attic ἔσῃ) with doubled σ. ἔτι δήν is 'any longer', literally 'still for long'; τοι is 'for you'.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γάρ σε μνῶνται ἀριστῆες κατὰ δῆμον
πάντων Φαιήκων, ὅθι τοι γένος ἐστὶ καὶ αὐτῇ.
sentences.l:
for already you are wooed by the best men throughout the land
of all the Phaeacians, where you also have your family.
sentences.i: for already the best men of all the Phaeacians are courting you throughout the land, where you too have your family.
sentences.n: μνῶνται is from μνάομαι 'woo, court'. ἀριστῆες, 'the best men', are the leading nobles. κατὰ δῆμον is 'throughout the land'. ὅθι is 'where'; its ending -θι marks place. In ὅθι τοι γένος ἐστὶ καὶ αὐτῇ, γένος is 'family, descent' and καὶ αὐτῇ means 'you yourself too': the suitors come from her own people, among whom her family belongs.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ἐπότρυνον πατέρα κλυτὸν ἠῶθι πρὸ
ἡμιόνους καὶ ἄμαξαν ἐφοπλίσαι, ἥ κεν ἄγῃσι
ζῶστρά τε καὶ πέπλους καὶ ῥήγεα σιγαλόεντα.
sentences.l:
But come, urge your famous father, at dawn, early,
mules and a wagon to make ready, which will carry
girdles and robes and glossy rugs.
sentences.i: But come, urge your famous father, early at dawn, to make ready the mules and a wagon, to carry the girdles and robes and glossy rugs.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come'. ἐπότρυνον is the imperative of ἐποτρύνω 'urge on', with the infinitive ἐφοπλίσαι 'to make ready'. κλυτόν is 'famous', the house word even where it sits oddly. ἠῶθι, with the place-ending -θι, and πρό as an adverb give 'early, at dawn'. ἄμαξα here and ἀπήνη below are two words for the same mule-wagon, and both are rendered 'wagon'. ἥ is the relative 'which', feminine to agree with ἄμαξαν, and κεν ἄγῃσι is a subjunctive with the old ending -ῃσι: 'that will carry'. ζῶστρα are girdles, πέπλοι robes, ῥήγεα woollen rugs or coverlets, and σιγαλόεντα belongs with the rugs.

sentences.t:
καὶ δὲ σοὶ ὧδ’ αὐτῇ πολὺ κάλλιον ἠὲ πόδεσσιν
ἔρχεσθαι·
sentences.l:
For also for you yourself thus much finer than on foot
to go;
sentences.i: And it is much better for you yourself to go like this than on foot;
sentences.n: καὶ δέ is a compound particle, 'and also, moreover'. κάλλιον is the comparative of καλός, used as an adverb with ἐστί understood, and ἠέ is 'than'. πόδεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσιν: 'on foot'. ὧδε is 'in this way', that is riding in the wagon.

sentences.t: πολλὸν γὰρ ἀπὸ πλυνοί εἰσι πόληος.
sentences.l: for far from the city are the washing-places.”
sentences.i: for the washing-places are a long way from the city.”
sentences.n: πολλόν is an adverb, 'far'; ἀπό stands apart from its genitive πόληος, the epic genitive of πόλις (Attic πόλεως). πλυνοί are the washing-places, troughs or pools; they are described at line 86.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἀπέβη γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη
Οὔλυμπόνδ’, ὅθι φασὶ θεῶν ἕδος ἀσφαλὲς αἰεὶ
ἔμμεναι.
sentences.l:
She then, so having spoken, went away, gleaming-eyed Athena,
to Olympus, where they say the seat of the gods, secure, always
to be.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and gleaming-eyed Athena went away to Olympus, where, they say, the seat of the gods stands secure for ever.
sentences.n: The first line is word for word 1.319. Οὔλυμπόνδ’ has the suffix -δε of direction, 'to Olympus'. ὅθι φασί is 'where, they say'; ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί (Attic εἶναι) in the reported statement. ἀσφαλές, 'secure, not to be tripped up', is built on ἀ- and σφάλλω; αἰεί is ἀεί.

sentences.t:
οὔτ’ ἀνέμοισι τινάσσεται οὔτε ποτ’ ὄμβρῳ
δεύεται οὔτε χιὼν ἐπιπίλναται, ἀλλὰ μάλ’ αἴθρη
πέπταται ἀνέφελος, λευκὴ δ’ ἐπιδέδρομεν αἴγλη·
sentences.i: Winds never shake it, no rain wets it, no snow comes near, but a wholly clear sky is spread about it, cloudless, and white radiance has run over it;
sentences.n: The subject throughout is ἕδος, 'the seat'. οὔτε … οὔτε … οὔτε is 'neither … nor … nor'. ἀνέμοισι is a dative plural in -οισι. δεύεται is 'is wetted' (δεύω) and ἐπιπίλναται 'draws near'. πέπταται, perfect passive of πετάννυμι 'spread out', and ἐπιδέδρομεν, perfect of ἐπιτρέχω 'run over', give a lasting state: 'has been spread, has run over and stays so'. αἴθρη is a clear sky, ἀνέφελος 'cloudless'.

sentences.t: τῷ ἔνι τέρπονται μάκαρες θεοὶ ἤματα πάντα.
sentences.l: In this delight the blessed gods all their days.
sentences.i: The blessed gods take their pleasure in it for all their days.
sentences.n: τῷ ἔνι stands for ἐν τῷ, 'in it' (the seat), with the preposition after its pronoun. τέρπονται is 'take delight'. μάκαρες, 'blessed', is the word used of the gods as against mortals. ἤματα πάντα is an accusative of duration, 'all their days'.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ἀπέβη γλαυκῶπις, ἐπεὶ διεπέφραδε κούρῃ.
sentences.l: There she went away, the gleaming-eyed one, when she had made it plain to the maiden.
sentences.i: There the gleaming-eyed goddess went, when she had made all this plain to the girl.
sentences.n: γλαυκῶπις stands alone for Athena, the epithet doing the work of the name, with the house rendering 'gleaming-eyed'. ἔνθα is 'thither, there'. διεπέφραδε is a reduplicated aorist of διαφράζω 'point out, explain': the plan has been laid out to the girl.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ Ἠὼς ἦλθεν ἐύθρονος, ἥ μιν ἔγειρε
Ναυσικάαν ἐύπεπλον·
sentences.l:
Straightway came Dawn, fair-throned, who woke her,
Nausicaa, fair-robed;
sentences.i: At once fair-throned Dawn came, and woke fair-robed Nausicaa;
sentences.n: Ἠώς is the goddess Dawn. ἐύθρονος, 'fair-throned' (θρόνος 'seat'), is her stock epithet, and ἐύπεπλος, 'fair-robed' (πέπλος 'robe'), is Nausicaa’s; ἐύ- is rendered 'fair' in both. μιν … Ναυσικάαν sets the pronoun 'her' beside the name it stands for, a common epic way of adding the name as a clarification. ἔγειρε is the imperfect of ἐγείρω 'wake'.

sentences.t:
ἄφαρ δ’ ἀπεθαύμασ’ ὄνειρον,
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι διὰ δώμαθ’, ἵν’ ἀγγείλειε τοκεῦσιν,
πατρὶ φίλῳ καὶ μητρί·
sentences.i: and at once she marvelled at her dream, and set out through the house to tell her parents, her dear father and her mother;
sentences.n: ἀπεθαύμασ’ is the aorist of ἀποθαυμάζω 'wonder at'. βῆ δ’ ἰέναι, 'set out to go', is the phrase of line 15, with the ordinary infinitive ἰέναι where line 15 has ἴμεν. δώμαθ’ is δώματα, the rooms of the house. ἵν’ ἀγγείλειε is ἵνα with the optative, a purpose clause after a past tense: 'that she might tell'. τοκεῦσιν is the dative plural of τοκεύς 'parent'.

sentences.t: κιχήσατο δ’ ἔνδον ἐόντας·
sentences.l: and she came upon them being within;
sentences.i: She found them indoors;
sentences.n: κιχήσατο, from κιχάνω 'come upon, find', is an aorist middle in -σα- with no augment (Attic ἐκιχήσατο). ἔνδον ἐόντας is 'being inside', with ἐόντας the epic participle of εἰμί (Attic ὄντας). The next lines describe the two parents in turn.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν ἐπ’ ἐσχάρῃ ἧστο σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξὶν
ἠλάκατα στρωφῶσ’ ἁλιπόρφυρα·
sentences.l:
she, on the one hand, by the hearth was sitting with her attendant women,
turning sea-purple yarn;
sentences.i: She was sitting by the hearth with her attendant women, turning sea-purple yarn;
sentences.n: ἡ μέν is 'she', the mother, set against τῷ δέ, the father, in the next unit. ἐσχάρη is the hearth; ἧστο is the imperfect of ἧμαι 'sit'. ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξίν is 'attendant women', with the dative endings -οισι and -ξίν. στρωφῶσ’ is στρωφῶσα, the feminine participle of στρωφάω 'turn, twirl'. ἠλάκατα is the neuter plural of a word tied to ἠλακάτη 'distaff': the wool being spun or the yarn spun from it; which of the two is meant is not certain. ἁλιπόρφυρα is 'sea-purple' (ἅλς + πορφύρα), wool dyed with the purple that came from the sea.

sentences.t:
τῷ δὲ θύραζε
ἐρχομένῳ ξύμβλητο μετὰ κλειτοὺς βασιλῆας
ἐς βουλήν, ἵνα μιν κάλεον Φαίηκες ἀγαυοί.
sentences.l:
and to him, as he was going
out of doors, she came up, to go among the famous kings
to the council, where were calling him the noble Phaeacians.
sentences.i: and she met him as he was going out of doors to join the famous kings in the council, where the noble Phaeacians were calling him.
sentences.n: ξύμβλητο is the aorist middle of ξυμβάλλω (Attic συμβάλλω) 'meet', taking the dative τῷ … ἐρχομένῳ 'him as he went'; the subject is Nausicaa. θύραζε has the direction-ending -ζε (= -δε): 'out of doors'. κλειτούς is the same word as κλυτούς, 'famous'; the βασιλῆες are the Phaeacian chiefs. κάλεον is an imperfect, uncontracted (Attic ἐκάλουν). Φαίηκες ἀγαυοί is 'the noble Phaeacians', with ἀγαυός as 'noble'.

sentences.t: ἡ δὲ μάλ’ ἄγχι στᾶσα φίλον πατέρα προσέειπε·
sentences.l: and she, very near standing, her dear father addressed:
sentences.i: She stood very close to her dear father and addressed him:
sentences.n: στᾶσα is the aorist participle of ἵστημι, 'having taken her stand'; μάλ’ ἄγχι is 'very near'. προσέειπε is the house verb 'addressed'. The speech runs from 57 to 65.

sentences.l:
“Dear papa, would you not make ready for me a wagon,
high, well-wheeled, that I may take my famous clothes
to the river, to wash them, which for me lie soiled?
sentences.i: “Dear papa, will you not make ready a high, well-wheeled wagon for me, so that I can take my famous clothes to the river to wash them, which lie there soiled?
sentences.n: πάππα is a child’s word for father, 'papa'; φίλ’ is φίλε elided. οὐκ ἂν … ἐφοπλίσσειας is the optative with ἄν as a polite request: 'would you not make ready?' ἐύκυκλος is 'well-wheeled' (κύκλος 'wheel'). ἵνα … ἄγωμαι takes a short-vowel subjunctive: 'so that I may take'. κλυτά, 'famous', keeps the house word even for clothes. πλυνέουσα is the future participle 'to wash', as at line 31. ῥερυπωμένα is a perfect passive participle of ῥυπόω 'make dirty', with epic ῥε- reduplication: 'soiled'.

sentences.t:
καὶ δὲ σοὶ αὐτῷ ἔοικε μετὰ πρώτοισιν ἐόντα
βουλὰς βουλεύειν καθαρὰ χροΐ εἵματ’ ἔχοντα.
sentences.l:
And also for you yourself it is fitting, among the first being,
counsels to counsel, clean clothes on your skin having.
sentences.i: And it is fitting for you yourself, being among the foremost, to take counsel with clean clothes on your body.
sentences.n: ἔοικε is impersonal, 'it is fitting', with an infinitive. ἐόντα and ἔχοντα are accusatives agreeing with the unstated subject of the infinitive, 'you'. μετὰ πρώτοισιν is 'among the foremost men'. βουλὰς βουλεύειν, 'to plan plans', pairs a noun with its own verb. χροΐ is the dative of χρώς 'skin, body'.

sentences.t:
πέντε δέ τοι φίλοι υἷες ἐνὶ μεγάροις γεγάασιν,
οἱ δύ’ ὀπυίοντες, τρεῖς δ’ ἠίθεοι θαλέθοντες·
sentences.l:
And five, for you, dear sons in the halls have been born,
of whom two are taking wives, and three unwed young men, blooming;
sentences.i: You have five dear sons in your halls, two of them married and three unwed young men in full bloom;
sentences.n: πέντε … υἷες is 'five sons' and τοι 'you have'; ἐνὶ μεγάροις is 'in the halls'. γεγάασιν is the Homeric perfect of γίγνομαι (Attic γεγόνασι), 'have been born, are'. ὀπυίοντες, from ὀπυίω 'take to wife', means 'married'. ἠίθεοι are unmarried young men, and θαλέθοντες, from θαλέθω 'bloom, thrive', 'in the bloom of youth'.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ αἰεὶ ἐθέλουσι νεόπλυτα εἵματ’ ἔχοντες
ἐς χορὸν ἔρχεσθαι·
sentences.l:
and they always wish, newly washed clothes wearing,
to go to the dance;
sentences.i: and they always want to go to the dance wearing freshly washed clothes;
sentences.n: νεόπλυτα is 'freshly washed' (νέος + πλυτός, from πλύνω). ἔχοντες, 'having', means wearing. ἐθέλουσι takes the infinitive: 'want to'. ἐς χορόν is 'to the dance'; χορός is both the dancing-place and the dancers.

sentences.t: τὰ δ’ ἐμῇ φρενὶ πάντα μέμηλεν.
sentences.l: and these things all in my mind are a care.”
sentences.i: and all this is a care to my mind.”
sentences.n: τά is 'these things', the article as a demonstrative. μέμηλεν is the perfect of μέλω 'be a care', with the dative ἐμῇ φρενί: 'to my mind'.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’·
sentences.l: So she spoke;
sentences.i: So she spoke;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is ὣς ἔφατο, the closing formula 'so she spoke', with ἔφατο an augmented imperfect middle of φημί. The pause after it sets off the explanation that follows.

sentences.t:
αἴδετο γὰρ θαλερὸν γάμον ἐξονομῆναι
πατρὶ φίλῳ.
sentences.l:
for she was ashamed a blooming marriage to name
to her dear father.
sentences.i: for she felt shame at naming her blooming marriage to her dear father.
sentences.n: αἴδετο is the imperfect of αἰδέομαι 'feel shame'. γάρ gives the reason for what she left out: she spoke of the washing and the clothes and did not say the word 'marriage'. θαλερός is 'blooming, lusty'. ἐξονομῆναι is an aorist infinitive of ἐξονομαίνω 'name out, speak of'. πατρὶ φίλῳ is a dative, 'to her dear father'.

sentences.t: ὁ δὲ πάντα νόει καὶ ἀμείβετο μύθῳ·
sentences.l: but he understood everything, and answered in speech:
sentences.i: But he understood everything and answered her:
sentences.n: ὁ is 'he', the father, the article as a pronoun. νόει is the imperfect of νοέω 'perceive, understand': he saw what she had not said. ἀμείβετο is 'answered'; μύθῳ is the dative 'with words'.

sentences.t: οὔτε τοι ἡμιόνων φθονέω, τέκος, οὔτε τευ ἄλλου.
sentences.l: “Neither of the mules do I begrudge you, child, nor of anything else.
sentences.i: “I do not begrudge you the mules, child, nor anything else.
sentences.n: φθονέω, 'begrudge', takes a genitive of the thing: ἡμιόνων 'of the mules'; τοι is 'to you'. τέκος 'child' is a neuter noun used as an affectionate address. τευ is an epic and Ionic form of τινός, 'of anything', so 'nor of anything else'.

sentences.t: ἔρχευ·
sentences.l: Go;
sentences.i: Go;
sentences.n: ἔρχευ is the imperative of ἔρχομαι 'go', from the older ἔρχεο with the vowels run together (Attic ἔρχου). The single word is a whole sentence; the pause after it is Murray’s.

sentences.t:
ἀτάρ τοι δμῶες ἐφοπλίσσουσιν ἀπήνην
ὑψηλὴν ἐύκυκλον, ὑπερτερίῃ ἀραρυῖαν.
sentences.l:
but for you the servants are making ready the wagon,
high, well-wheeled, fitted with an upper frame.”
sentences.i: but the servants will make the wagon ready for you, a high, well-wheeled wagon with an upper frame fitted to it.”
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is 'but, and yet'. δμῶες are the household servants. The present ἐφοπλίσσουσιν has the force of an immediate future: 'are making ready'. ὑψηλὴν ἐύκυκλον is the pair of words of line 58, kept in the same English, 'high, well-wheeled'. ἀραρυῖαν is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω 'fit together', 'fitted with'. The meaning of ὑπερτερίη is not certain: it is taken to be the upper part of the wagon, a top rail or covering, and 'upper frame' is only a guess.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν δμώεσσιν ἐκέκλετο, τοὶ δ’ ἐπίθοντο.
sentences.l: So having spoken, to the servants he called out, and they obeyed.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and gave orders to the servants, and they obeyed.
sentences.n: δμώεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσιν, 'to the servants'. ἐκέκλετο, from κέλομαι 'call on, order', is an aorist with epic reduplication. τοί (in τοὶ δ’) is 'they', the article as a pronoun. ἐπίθοντο is an aorist middle of πείθομαι 'obey'.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐκτὸς ἄμαξαν ἐύτροχον ἡμιονείην
ὥπλεον, ἡμιόνους θ’ ὕπαγον ζεῦξάν θ’ ὑπ’ ἀπήνῃ·
sentences.l:
They then outside a wagon, well-rolling, mule-drawn,
prepared, and the mules led up, and yoked them under the wagon;
sentences.i: Outside, they made ready the well-rolling, mule-drawn wagon, brought the mules up and yoked them to the wagon;
sentences.n: οἱ μέν is 'they', the servants. ἐκτός is 'outside' the house. ἄμαξαν and ἀπήνῃ name the same wagon and are both 'wagon'. ἐύτροχος is 'well-rolling' (from τροχός 'wheel'), and ἡμιονείην 'drawn by mules'. ὥπλεον is the imperfect of ὁπλέω 'make ready'. ὕπαγον is 'led up under', and ζεῦξαν the aorist of ζεύγνυμι 'yoke'; ὑπ’ ἀπήνῃ, 'under the wagon', is the idiom for yoking the animals to it.

sentences.t: κούρη δ’ ἐκ θαλάμοιο φέρεν ἐσθῆτα φαεινήν.
sentences.l: and the maiden from the chamber brought clothing, shining.
sentences.i: and the maiden brought the shining clothes out of her chamber.
sentences.n: θαλάμοιο is a genitive in -οιο (= -ου), 'from the chamber'. φέρεν is an imperfect without augment. ἐσθῆτα is 'clothing' as a mass noun, with φαεινήν 'shining', as at line 19.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὴν μὲν κατέθηκεν ἐυξέστῳ ἐπ’ ἀπήνῃ,
μήτηρ δ’ ἐν κίστῃ ἐτίθει μενοεικέ’ ἐδωδὴν
παντοίην, ἐν δ’ ὄψα τίθει, ἐν δ’ οἶνον ἔχευεν
ἀσκῷ ἐν αἰγείῳ·
sentences.l:
And it she set down on the well-polished wagon,
but her mother in a chest put satisfying food
of every kind, and in put relishes, and in poured wine
into a goatskin;
sentences.i: and she laid it on the well-polished wagon; her mother put satisfying food of every kind into a chest, added relishes to it, and poured wine into a goatskin;
sentences.n: τήν is 'it', the article as a pronoun, the clothing. ἐύξεστος, 'well-polished', is from ξέω 'scrape, plane'. ἐν … τίθει and ἐν … ἔχευεν are tmesis, 'put in' and 'poured in', the preverb standing apart from its verb. μενοεικής is 'satisfying the appetite'. ὄψον is the relish eaten with bread, such as meat, fish or cheese. ἀσκός is a skin bag, αἴγειος 'of a goat', κίστη a chest or basket.

sentences.t: κούρη δ’ ἐπεβήσετ’ ἀπήνης.
sentences.l: and the maiden mounted the wagon.
sentences.i: and the girl climbed onto the wagon.
sentences.n: ἐπεβήσετο is an aorist middle of ἐπιβαίνω 'step onto', in a -σε- form; verbs of mounting take the genitive, here ἀπήνης.

sentences.t:
δῶκεν δὲ χρυσέῃ ἐν ληκύθῳ ὑγρὸν ἔλαιον,
ἧος χυτλώσαιτο σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξίν.
sentences.l:
and she gave in a golden oil-flask liquid olive oil,
so that she might anoint herself with her attendant women.
sentences.i: Her mother also gave her liquid olive oil in a golden flask, so that she might anoint herself along with her attendant women.
sentences.n: The subject of δῶκεν is still the mother. χρυσέῃ is Ionic for χρυσῇ 'golden'. ληκύθος is an oil-flask and ὑγρὸν ἔλαιον 'liquid olive oil'. ἧος is the epic form of ἕως, here 'so that'. χυτλώσαιτο is an aorist optative middle of χυτλόομαι 'anoint oneself with oil', the optative after a past tense. Anointing after a bath is the custom (compare line 96).

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἔλαβεν μάστιγα καὶ ἡνία σιγαλόεντα,
μάστιξεν δ’ ἐλάαν·
sentences.l:
and she took the whip and the glossy reins,
and she whipped them to drive on;
sentences.i: She took the whip and the glossy reins, and whipped them to drive them on;
sentences.n: ἡ is 'she', Nausicaa. ἡνία is the plural of ἡνίον, 'reins'; σιγαλόεντα is 'glossy', as at 26 and 38. μάστιξεν ἐλάαν is 'she whipped to drive', with ἐλάαν the uncontracted infinitive of ἐλαύνω; the clause also opens 3.484 and 3.494.

sentences.t: καναχὴ δ’ ἦν ἡμιόνοιιν.
sentences.l: and there was a clatter of the two mules.
sentences.i: and there was a clatter from the two mules.
sentences.n: ἡμιόνοιιν is a dual genitive in -οιιν, 'of the two mules': a pair draws the wagon. καναχή is a ringing or clattering noise.

sentences.t:
αἱ δ’ ἄμοτον τανύοντο, φέρον δ’ ἐσθῆτα καὶ αὐτήν,
οὐκ οἴην, ἅμα τῇ γε καὶ ἀμφίπολοι κίον ἄλλαι.
sentences.l:
and they unceasingly stretched themselves, and carried the clothing and her herself,
not alone; with her too went other attendants.
sentences.i: The mules strained on without pause, carrying the clothes and Nausicaa herself, and she was not alone, for other attendants went with her.
sentences.n: αἱ δ’ is 'they', feminine, the mules. τανύοντο, from τανύομαι 'stretch oneself', is 'strained at the pull'. ἄμοτον is an adverb whose exact sense is not known; 'unceasingly' is the traditional guess. καὶ αὐτήν is 'and her herself', Nausicaa as well as the clothes. οὐκ οἴην is 'not alone' (οἶος). κίον is an unaugmented imperfect of κίω 'go'; ἅμα τῇ γε is 'along with her', τῇ being the article as a pronoun.

sentences.t:
αἱ δ’ ὅτε δὴ ποταμοῖο ῥόον περικαλλέ’ ἵκοντο,
ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι πλυνοὶ ἦσαν ἐπηετανοί, πολὺ δ’ ὕδωρ
καλὸν ὑπεκπρόρεεν μάλα περ ῥυπόωντα καθῆραι,
ἔνθ’ αἵ γ’ ἡμιόνους μὲν ὑπεκπροέλυσαν ἀπήνης.
sentences.l:
And when they came to the very fair stream of the river,
there indeed were washing-places, never-failing, and much water
fair flowed forth from beneath, enough to clean even very filthy things,
there they the mules unyoked from the wagon.
sentences.i: When they came to the very fair stream of the river, where the washing-places were, never-failing, and plenty of fair water flowed forth from beneath, enough to clean even the filthiest things, there they unyoked the mules from the wagon.
sentences.n: One sentence: a ὅτε clause, then two ἔνθα clauses. ῥόον, 'stream', is the object of ἵκοντο, an unaugmented form of ἱκνέομαι 'arrive at'. περικαλλέ’ is περικαλλέα, 'very fair' (περι- as an intensive). ἐπηετανός is 'never-failing'; the word’s exact sense (perhaps 'lasting all the year') is only approximately known. ὑπεκπρόρεεν has three preverbs, ὑπό, ἐκ, πρό: 'flowed forth from under'. ῥυπόωντα is an uncontracted participle of ῥυπόω 'be dirty', and καθῆραι, the aorist infinitive of καθαίρω, expresses result: 'enough to clean'. ὑπεκπροέλυσαν, 'loosed out from under', is the same triple compound used for unyoking; ἀπήνης is a genitive of separation.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰς μὲν σεῦαν ποταμὸν πάρα δινήεντα
τρώγειν ἄγρωστιν μελιηδέα·
sentences.l:
and them they drove along the eddying river
to graze on honey-sweet grass;
sentences.i: and drove them along the eddying river to graze on the honey-sweet grass;
sentences.n: τάς is 'them', the mules, the article as a pronoun. σεῦαν is an aorist of σεύω 'drive, chase'. πάρα is παρά placed after its noun (accent thrown back): 'along the river'. δινήεις is 'eddying' (δίνη 'eddy'). τρώγειν, 'to gnaw, munch', gives the purpose. ἄγρωστις is a kind of grass. μελιηδής is 'honey-sweet' (μέλι + ἡδύς).

sentences.t:
ταὶ δ’ ἀπ’ ἀπήνης
εἵματα χερσὶν ἕλοντο καὶ ἐσφόρεον μέλαν ὕδωρ,
στεῖβον δ’ ἐν βόθροισι θοῶς ἔριδα προφέρουσαι.
sentences.l:
and they, from the wagon,
took the clothes in their hands and carried in dark water,
and trod them in the pits swiftly, rivalry putting forward.
sentences.i: while they took the clothes from the wagon in their hands and carried dark water in, and trod them swiftly in the pits, each trying to outdo the other.
sentences.n: ταὶ δ’ is 'and they', the girls; ταί is the feminine plural article as a pronoun. ἕλοντο is an aorist middle of αἱρέω, 'took for themselves'. ἐσφόρεον is the imperfect of ἐσφορέω 'carry in'; we take μέλαν ὕδωρ, 'dark water', as its object, carried into the pits, though the Greek would also allow the clothes to be carried into the water. στεῖβον is 'trod, stamped' (στείβω): the clothes are washed by treading. βόθροισι is a dative plural, 'in pits'. θοῶς is 'swiftly'. ἔριδα προφέρουσαι, literally 'putting strife forward', is the phrase for competing: each tries to outdo the other.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πλῦνάν τε κάθηράν τε ῥύπα πάντα,
ἑξείης πέτασαν παρὰ θῖν’ ἁλός, ἧχι μάλιστα
λάιγγας ποτὶ χέρσον ἀποπλύνεσκε θάλασσα.
sentences.l:
But when they had washed and cleaned all the dirt,
in a row they spread them along the shore of the salt-sea, where especially
the sea used to wash the pebbles clean toward the dry land.
sentences.i: When they had washed and cleaned off all the dirt, they laid the clothes out in a row along the shore of the sea, where the sea most washed the pebbles clean against the land.
sentences.n: πλῦνάν and κάθηράν are unaugmented aorists of πλύνω 'wash' and καθαίρω 'clean'; ῥύπα is the neuter plural of ῥύπος 'dirt'. ἑξείης is 'in order, in a row'. πέτασαν is an aorist of πετάννυμι 'spread out' (the clothes, to dry). θῖν’ is θῖνα, the accusative of θίς 'shore, beach'. ἧχι is 'where'. ἀποπλύνεσκε has the iterative suffix -σκ-, 'used to wash clean'. λάιγγας are pebbles, ποτί is πρός 'toward', and χέρσον is 'dry land'.

sentences.t:
αἱ δὲ λοεσσάμεναι καὶ χρισάμεναι λίπ’ ἐλαίῳ
δεῖπνον ἔπειθ’ εἵλοντο παρ’ ὄχθῃσιν ποταμοῖο,
εἵματα δ’ ἠελίοιο μένον τερσήμεναι αὐγῇ.
sentences.l:
And they, having bathed and having anointed themselves richly with oil,
then took their meal beside the banks of the river,
and waited for the clothes to dry in the sun’s ray.
sentences.i: Then, when they had bathed and anointed themselves richly with oil, they took their meal on the banks of the river and waited for the clothes to dry in the light of the sun.
sentences.n: λοεσσάμεναι (aorist middle participle of λούω 'bathe') and χρισάμεναι (χρίω 'anoint') are the girls’ own bath and oil-rub. λίπ’ is λίπα, an adverb 'richly, sleekly', with the dative ἐλαίῳ. εἵλοντο is an aorist middle of αἱρέω, 'took for themselves'. ὄχθῃσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν. τερσήμεναι is an infinitive in -μεναι from τέρσομαι 'become dry', after μένον 'waited'. ἠελίοιο is a genitive in -οιο; αὐγή is a ray or gleam.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ σίτου τάρφθεν δμῳαί τε καὶ αὐτή,
σφαίρῃ ταὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπαιζον, ἀπὸ κρήδεμνα βαλοῦσαι·
sentences.l:
But when they had had their fill of food, the maidservants and she herself,
at ball they then played, their head-veils having cast off;
sentences.i: When the maids and she herself had had their fill of food, they cast off their head-veils and played at ball;
sentences.n: τάρφθεν is an aorist passive of τέρπω 'satisfy', 'were satisfied with', and takes the genitive σίτου 'food'. δμῳαί are maidservants. αὐτή is 'she herself', Nausicaa. σφαίρῃ is the dative of σφαῖρα 'ball'. The δέ of ταὶ δ’ ἄρ’ opens the main clause after the ἐπεί clause. ἀπὸ … βαλοῦσαι is a tmesis, 'having thrown off'. κρήδεμνα are head-veils.

sentences.t: τῇσι δὲ Ναυσικάα λευκώλενος ἤρχετο μολπῆς.
sentences.l: and for them white-armed Nausicaa led off the song-and-dance.
sentences.i: and white-armed Nausicaa led the song and dance for them.
sentences.n: τῇσι is a feminine dative plural, the article as a pronoun: 'for them'. ἄρχομαι with the genitive means 'begin', so ἤρχετο μολπῆς is 'led off the song-and-dance'; μολπή is singing with dancing. λευκώλενος is 'white-armed' (λευκός 'white' + ὠλένη 'forearm').

sentences.t:
οἵη δ’ Ἄρτεμις εἶσι κατ’ οὔρεα ἰοχέαιρα,
ἢ κατὰ Τηΰγετον περιμήκετον ἢ Ἐρύμανθον,
τερπομένη κάπροισι καὶ ὠκείῃς ἐλάφοισι·
sentences.i: As Artemis, who showers her arrows, ranges over the mountains, along the very long ridge of Taygetus or over Erymanthus, delighting in boars and swift deer;
sentences.n: A simile begins: οἵη δέ is 'as when', and the comparison is completed by ὣς ἥ γ’ in line 109. εἶσι, from εἶμι, is 'goes', of what she habitually does. οὔρεα is the epic plural of ὄρος. ἰοχέαιρα is Artemis’ epithet; its second element is disputed (χέω 'pour', giving 'who showers arrows', or χαίρω, 'who delights in arrows'), and the house English follows the first with the doubt stated. Taygetus and Erymanthus are mountains. περιμήκετον is 'very long' (περι- as an intensive). τερπομένη 'delighting' takes the datives κάπροισι 'boars' and ἐλάφοισι 'deer'; ὠκείῃς is an old dative plural in -ῃς (= ὠκείαις) of ὠκύς 'swift'.

sentences.t:
τῇ δέ θ’ ἅμα νύμφαι, κοῦραι Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο,
ἀγρονόμοι παίζουσι, γέγηθε δέ τε φρένα Λητώ·
sentences.l:
and with her together the nymphs, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus,
field-ranging, play, and rejoices in her mind Leto;
sentences.i: and with her the nymphs, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, who range the countryside, play, and Leto is glad in her mind;
sentences.n: τῇ is 'with her' (ἅμα + dative), the article as a pronoun; δέ θ’ is δέ τε, and the epic τε marks what is habitual in a simile. κοῦραι Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο is 'daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus'; the meaning of αἰγίοχος is disputed, and the house English is 'aegis-bearing'. ἀγρονόμοι, 'field-ranging' (ἀγρός 'field' + νέμομαι 'range'), describes the nymphs of the countryside. γέγηθε is the perfect of γηθέω 'rejoice'; φρένα is an accusative of respect, 'in her mind'. Leto is the mother of Artemis.

sentences.t:
πασάων δ’ ὑπὲρ ἥ γε κάρη ἔχει ἠδὲ μέτωπα,
ῥεῖά τ’ ἀριγνώτη πέλεται, καλαὶ δέ τε πᾶσαι·
sentences.l:
and above all of them she holds head and brow,
and easily recognisable she is, and fair too are all of them;
sentences.i: and she holds her head and brow above them all, and is easily known, though all of them are fair;
sentences.n: πασάων is the epic genitive plural in -άων (Attic πασῶν), governed by ὑπέρ: 'above them all'. κάρη … μέτωπα, 'head and brow', is what she carries above the rest, so she stands out by the head. ἥ γε is 'she', with emphasis. ἀριγνώτη is 'easily known' (ἀρι- as an intensive + γιγνώσκω) and ῥεῖα 'easily'; πέλεται is a poetic 'is'. The second τε again marks a general truth, and δέ τε … πᾶσαι comes out 'though all are fair'.

sentences.t: ὣς ἥ γ’ ἀμφιπόλοισι μετέπρεπε παρθένος ἀδμής.
sentences.l: So she among her attendants stood out, the unwed maiden.
sentences.i: So she stood out among her attendants, the unwed maiden.
sentences.n: ὣς ἥ γ’ closes the simile begun at line 102: 'as Artemis … so she'. μετέπρεπε, imperfect of μεταπρέπω 'be conspicuous among', takes the dative ἀμφιπόλοισι. ἀδμής, from ἀ- 'not' and δάμνημι 'tame, subdue', means 'untamed', hence 'unwed'.
